Ananta-śayana
(‘One who is reclining on the serpent अनन्त’)
------------------------------------------
Lord विष्णु has several aspects of manifestation. The one depicting him as reclining on the coils of serpent शेष or अनन्त (as bed) is called ‘Śeṣaśayana’ or ‘Anantaśayana.’
The śayana-images (images showing विष्णु, in the reclining posture) are of four types: yogaśayana, bhogaśayana, vīraśayana and ābhicārikaśayana. The first shows him with two arms and in a meditative mood, with half—closed eyes. Instead of Śrī and Bhū, the two consorts, the sages भृगु and मार्कण्डेय are shown. ब्रह्मा is shown seated on the lotus emerging from his navel. In the second type there are four arms and the icon is fully bedecked with ornaments. Śrī and Bhū are also shown along with the sages भृगु and मार्कण्डेय. ब्रह्मा and शिव are shown on the rear wall. In the third type, he is holding शङ्ख (conch) and चक्र (discus) in two of the four hands. The demons मधु and कैटभ are shown at his feet, trying to attack him. In the last type, he is shown with an emaciated body, scanty clothing and with no attendants. This image is usually set up outside the town or village.
These four images are respectively worshipped by those seeking spiritual welfare, worldly enjoyments, strength and destruction of enemies.
Trivandrum, capital city of Kerala state, was formerly known as Tiru-अनन्त-puram or Anantaśayana since it has a reputed temple dedicated to अनन्त-शयन, also called Padmanābha. It is one of the well-known shrines dedicated to विष्णु and was probably built during the early medieval era. The image is made of stucco and hence no अभिषेक (ceremonial bathing) is done to it.
The main difference between the रङ्गनाथ icon (which is also a śayana—image) and Anantaśayana is that the latter has ब्रह्मा on the lotus rising from the navel whereas the former does not have it.

Anāsakti-yoga
(‘Yoga of disinterestedness,’ ‘Yoga of detachment’)
------------------------------------------
The dominant trend of the उपनिषद्स् is towards कर्म-सṁन्यास or कर्म-त्याग, renunication of all actions, since it was strongly believed that कर्म or action lead to spiritual bondage. Opposition to this view is first noticed in the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad (2) which is later on developed in the Bhagavadgītā as a regular doctrine. It is āsakti or attachment to the fruits of actions that is really the cause of spiritual bondage. Hence, if actions can be performed with anāsakti or detachment, the sting or the binding taint, being thus taken away, the very same actions lead to purification of मिन्द् and spiritual enlightenment. This is ‘anāsakti-योग,’ योग or union with God, through anāsakti or detachment. This theory thus strikes a balance between कर्म (activity) and सṁन्यास (renunciation), between pravṛtti (activism) and निवृत्ति (withdrawal). For details see KARMAYOGA.
See also BHAGAVADGĪTĀ and NIṢKĀMA-KARMA.

Ānandāśrama Mudraṇālaya
------------------------------------------
This is one of the few pioneering institutions that has been dedicated to preserving and publishing old books and manuscripts dealing with Hindu scriptures and Indological subjects.
Ānandāśrama Mudraṇālaya at PuṇeIt was started at Pune in A.

by M. C. Apte who dedicated all his wealth for the new institution.
It is actively engaged in collecting and preserving old manuscripts and books and publishing them.
The building of the institution has a shrine dedicated to शिव where religious programmes are conducted.
Apart from a guest-होउसे there is also a hostel for boy-students.
So far, 188 books have been printed and 8000 Sanskrit manuscripts have been collected. The process of digitalising them to preserve them in CD’s is going on.

Ānandabodha
------------------------------------------
One of the well-known polemical writers of Advaita metaphysics, आनन्द-bodha (11th cent. A.D.) (also called आनन्द-bodhācārya and आनन्दबोध Bhaṭṭārakā-cārya) a disciple of विमुक्तात्मन् of the Iṣṭisiddhi fame (10th cent. A. D.) has four works to his credit: Nyāyamakaranda, Nyāyadīpāvalī, Pramāṇamālā and Śabda-nirṇaya Vyākhyā. The first of these is the most celebrated and has been commented upon by चित्सुख (13th cent. A. D.). The special features of this work are: refutation of the Sāṅkhyan theory of multiplicity of selves and the apparent difference of objective entities; the theory that everything other than ब्रह्मन् is मिथ्या (false) since it is दृश्य (perceived); a new defini-tion of mithyātva (falsity) viz., sadbhinnatvaṁ mithyātvam (falsity is being diffe-rent from the real); that अविद्या is positive in the sense it is non-negative; that the cessation of अविद्या is an entity of a fifth category, different from sat (real), असत् (unreal), sad-असत् (real-unreal) and अनिर्वचनीय (indefinable).

anāhatanāda
(‘sound produced without beating’)
------------------------------------------
When a योगि practises prāṇā yāma (breathing exercises aimed at regulating the energy of प्राण) and achieves purification of the nāḍīs (tubular structures through which prāṇic energy flows) he starts hearing melodious sounds of प्रणव or Oṁkāra. Since these sounds are generated without any beating (āhati) of two objects (which, incidentally, is the usual way of producing sound) they are called ‘anāhata-नाद.’ The sound is normally heard through the right ear whether open or closed. However, it is more distinct when the ears are kept closed.
Some authorities say that the sound can also be heard if the ajapāmantra is repeated one lakh times.
See also जप">AJAPĀJAPA, NĀḌĪS and PRĀṆĀYĀMA.

Anasūyā
(‘one without jealousy’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most celebrated women of Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्, considered as a model of wifely virtues, अनसूया was a daughter of कर्दम and देवहूति. She was married to the great sage अत्रि whom she served with intense devotion and love. Once, when there was a severe famine, she saved people by producing vegetables and fruits through her power of तपस् (austerity). She even made the river गङ्गा which had dried up, flow again.
The Trinity (Brahmā, विष्णु and शिव) subjected her to a severe test of her chastity from which she emerged successfully. As a reward they were born as her children: विष्णु as दत्तात्रेय, शिव as दुर्वासस् and ब्रह्मा as चन्द्र.
When राम and सीता visited अत्रि’s hermitage in the दण्डक forest अनसूया taught सीता the value of devoted service to one’s husband as the necessary and sufficient discipline for spiritual welfare.
See also ATRI.

anavasthitatva
(‘instability’)
------------------------------------------
Patañjali, in his famous work, the Yogasūtras (1.30), describes nine anta-rāyas or obstacles to the attainment of योग. अनवस्थितत्व is the last in the list and also the most formidable one to overcome. With assiduous practice, a योगि can succeed in raising his मिन्द् to certain higher states but very soon it slides back to lower ones or reverts into the old rut. Deep-rooted evil tendencies like inordinate lust and love of lucre or mercurial irri-tability or crass selfishness are often responsible for this fall. By dispassionate and deep introspection, consultation with the गुरु and prayer to God, one can discover the root-cause and eliminate it.
See also ANTARĀYAS.

anāśramin
(‘One who has not adopted any आश्रम’)
------------------------------------------
According to the धर्मशास्त्रस्, the life of an individual is divided into four āśramas or stages of life viz., ब्रह्मचर्य, गार्हस्थ्य, वानप्रस्थ and सṁन्यास signifying the states of a student, होउसे-holder, forest-recluse and monk. It was obligatory for a householder belonging to the first three varṇas (castes) to maintain sacrificial fire and to offer oblations regularly. The wife also had a place in this ritual and could act as a substitute for her husband in times of need. No greater calamity could befall a householder than the untimely death of his wife. Her body would be cremated with the same fire in which she used to offer oblations. The widower had only two alternatives left: to enter into the next stage of the वानप्रस्थ or to marry once again and set up the fire afresh. Anyone who did neither was branded as an ‘anāśramin,’ one who was outside the pale of the आश्रम scheme. This was incompa-tible with the Vedic scheme of life.

Anna-sūkta
(‘hymn to ड़ोओद्’)
------------------------------------------
Anna or ड़ोओद्, which is responsible for sustenance, has always been looked upon with reverence in हिन्दुइस्म्. Offering of consecrated ड़ोओद् to the sacrificial fire is a common part of some rituals. It is especially so in the śrāddha (obsequies) ceremonies. In one such śrāddha, called pārvaṇa—śrāddha, after first consecrating the cooked ड़ोओद् meant for oblation into the fire, the rest of the ड़ोओद् in the vessel is also purified by the recitation of the Annasūkta.
The Annasūkta is a series of eleven verses taken from the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā (1.18

Ananta
(‘the endless’)
------------------------------------------
Literally the word means ‘that which is endless,’ hence ‘infinite’. It is one of the epithets frequently used to describe or praise God in the Hindu scriptures. The उपनिषद्स् hold that ब्रह्मन् is सत्य, ज्ञान and अनन्त (truth, knowledge or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and infinite).
In the mythological lore, आदिशेष the great serpent on whom Lord विष्णु is resting, is named ‘Ananta.’ He is ‘Ananta’ since he has an infinite number of hoods on which he is supporting the worlds. He represents cosmic time which is infinite and endless. Created worlds come into being in time and are sustained in time. This is the meaning of the hoods of अनन्त supporting the worlds.
See also ĀDIŚEṢA.

Annapūrṇā Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This Upaniṣad belongs to the Atharvaveda. It is a fairly long work of 337 verses spread over five chapters.
A योगि, Nidāgha by name, approaches Ṛbhu, the ‘best among knowers of ब्रह्मन्,’ for Self-knowledge. Ṛbhu prefaces his teaching by narrating how his ड़थेर् had taught him the ‘best of mantras,’ ‘the मन्त्र of अन्नपूर्णा’ of 27 letters (aim ह्रीṁ sauṁ śrīṁ klīm oṁ namo bhagavatyannapūrṇe mamābhilaṣitam annaṁ dehi svāhā), how he had pleased the Divine मोथेर् अन्नपूर्णा by repeating it day after day for a long time, how he had asked for आत्मज्ञान or Self-know-ledge from her when she appeared before him, and how he had got it by her grace. The name of the Upaniṣad is derived from this legend.
The rest of the Upaniṣad is just a long and loose discourse on Advaita philosophy in which many of its aspects have been brought in, though not in a systematic manner.
Apart from the topic of ‘bhrama’ (delusion) and how to overcome it, the Upaniṣad also deals with topics like vāsanākṣaya (destruction of tendencies carried over from the previous lives), manonāśa (dissolution of the मिन्द् through yogic exercises) and a detailed description of the jīvanmukta (‘the liberated in life’) who never gets affected by the various vicissitudes of life.
See also ADVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA and UPANIṢADS.

anārya
(‘non-Ārya’)
------------------------------------------
The words ārya and अनार्य, whatever their original connotations, lost their racial flavour in later literature. ‘Ārya’ is a well-bred man, a refined and cultured gentleman. अनार्य is the opposite of all these. The word was often used in a derogatory sense.
See also ĀRYA, DĀSA and DASYU.

Ananta-caturdaśī
(‘the fourteenth day connected with अनन्त’)
------------------------------------------
Vratas (religious vows) and utsavas (celebrations) have become an integral part of Hindu religious, cultural and social life. If vratas stress the need for personal religious vows and discipline, utsavas provide an opportunity for rejoicing with the other members of the community.
One of several such vratas is अनन्त-चतुर्दशी vrata, which is celebrated on the caturdaśī (14th day) of the bright fortnight of the month Bhādrapada (August-September). It consists chiefly in the worship of Lord विष्णु as अनन्त (‘the Infinite One’) and in the wearing of a holy strap of thread dyed with saffron, on the hand (on the right hand in the case of men and on the left in the case of women). The thread should be of cotton or silk and should have 14 knots. It should be worn after keeping it on a jar of water duly established on a मण्डल (ritual diagram) and worshipping it. The Agnipurāṇa (192.9) gives the मन्त्र to be recited on this occasion.
It is an individual vrata which is normally performed on the bank of a river. Salt is forbidden in this vrata. Gaining happiness is the result promised. It is believed that if it is performed regularly for 14 years, one can reach the abode of विष्णु.

Ānandagiri
------------------------------------------
Among all the Indian Philosophical systems, the Advaita Vedānta of शङ्कर and his followers can boast of the maximum number of written works. One of the writers in this line who has done yeomen service by writing sub-commentaries on all the major works of शङ्कर is आनन्द-ज्ञान, celebrated as आनन्दगिरि, who lived in the 14th cent. A. D. Known as Janārdana in his premonastic life, he was the son of one सूर्यनारायण and belonged to the country called Cera (now in Tamil Nadu). He was probably a devotee of विष्णु. His गुरु was Śuddhānanda. His ṭīkā (comment) on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Vārttika of सुरेश्वर (7th—8th cent. A.D.) has been highly appreciated. In his original polemical work Vedānta-तर्क-saṅgraha he has refuted the Vaiśeṣika categories like द्रव्य, गुण etc. In his conclusions he has tried to follow his predecessors like आनन्दबोध (11th cent. A. D.) and others. He holds that अविद्या or अज्ञान which is an indeterminable false entity is the stuff of this world. अज्ञान is one only and is supported by ब्रह्मन्.

Annapūrṇā
(‘filled with ड़ोओद्’)
------------------------------------------
If God is the creator of this universe, his power with which he creates, is pictured as a female deity, his consort, usually called शक्ति. Most of the female deities or goddesses of the Hindu pantheon are aspects of पार्वती, the consort of शिव, the third deity of the Hindu Trinity, responsible for destruction and dissolution of the universe.
Annapūrṇā, the possessor and giver of ड़ोओद्, is one of the important aspects of पार्वती. She got this name since she served अन्न or ड़ोओद् to Lord शिव himself when he was roaming about as a mendicant. She is shown as serving ड़ोओद् from a vessel of ruby.
Iconographically, she may be shown with four hands also, two hands holding पाश (noose) and परशु (battle-axe) and the other two showing the varada (boon-giving) and abhaya (protection from fear) mudrās.
Her worship ensures that the household will never lack ड़ोओद्. Her festival is usually observed in चैत्र (April), mostly in Bengal.
Her temple at काशी (Vārāṇasī, modern Banaras in Uttar Pradesh) is very famous.

ānandamayakośa
(‘the bliss sheath’)
------------------------------------------
One of the five sheaths, the pañca-kośas, it gets its name due to the experience of joy in सुषुप्ति or deep sleep. In content, it is identical with अज्ञान or nescience. Since it makes the जीव, the individual सोउल्, forget his nature as pure ‘caitanya’ or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, by covering it as it were, like a कोश or sheath, it is termed as a ‘kośa.’ It clings to the सोउल् till the state of लिबेरतिओन्.
See also PAÑCAKOŚAS.

annaprāśana
(‘feeding with cooked rice or ड़ोओद्’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu religious works known as धर्मशास्त्रस् consider the life of every Hindu as a religious process. It begins at conception and ends at च्रेमतिओन्. The individual’s life is to be purified, refined and sanctified continually by certain reli-gious processes called ‘saṁskāras,’ usually translated as ‘sacraments.’ They are sixteen in number. Hence the appellation ‘Ṣoḍaśa-सṁस्कारस्.’
Annaprāśana is the seventh in the list. It is the first feeding of the child with solid ड़ोओद्, starting the process of weaning the child away from breast-feeding. It can be performed any time after the sixth month and before the child completes one year.
The ड़थेर् prepares a ड़ोओद् of goat’s flesh or flesh of partridge or of fish or boiled rice depending upon the result he expects for the child, like nourishment or holy lustre and so on. One of these is mixed with curds, honey and ghee and the child is made to taste it with the reciting of certain Vedic hymns. Then the ड़थेर् offers oblations to the fire. The मोथेर् is to eat the remainder of the ड़ोओद्. होम may also be performed and feeding of the ब्राह्मणस् may be arranged.
According to some writers, on the day of this ceremony, tools and implements, vessels and weapons are to be spread in front of the gods worshipped in the होउसे and the child allowed to crawl among them. The first object seized by the child is said to indicate its future profession.
See also SAṀSKĀRAS and ṢOḌAŚA-SAṀSKĀRAS.

ānanda
(‘complete bliss’)
------------------------------------------
This term is generally used to indicate unadulterated perfect bliss, got by the realization of God or the Self. In fact, one of the three basic terms used to indicate the nature of God is आनन्द, the other two being sat (existence) and cit (consciousness). The second chapter of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad designated as Ānanda Vallī shows by a calculation of its own, that brahmānanda or bliss of ब्रह्मन् is infinitely superior to the greatest joy that a human being ideally situated in life can ever hope to get.
The word is also used to indicate Lord विष्णु, a particular variety of Sanskrit metre and particular combinations of nakṣatras (stars) with weekdays, like अश्विनी being in conjunction with Sunday, and so on.
The word is also used as a suffix in the names of saṁnyāsins (monks), though it is difficult to say since when exactly the practice began. Earlier saṁnyāsins like शङ्कर have not used it. Later ācāryas (pontiffs) of the Śṛṅgerī Monastery (for instance, Śaṅkarānanda) have started using it.

anna
(‘food’)
------------------------------------------
Anna or ड़ोओद् seems to be a favourite topic dealt with in the Hindu scriptures. The उपनिषद्स् have used the word times without number not only in the sense of physical ड़ोओद् but also to signify anything that is consumed or enjoyed. It stands for matter in general. In the long process of च्रेअतिओन् it is the lowest manifestation of the आत्मन्.
Anna nourishes not only the body but also the मिन्द्. Hence the stress on purity of ड़ोओद्.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् consider even eating as a religious act and give several rules concerning it.
See also ĀHĀRA and ĀHĀRAŚUDDHI.

anāhatacakra
(‘unbeaten sound plexus’)
------------------------------------------
It is one of the six centres of psychic energy mentioned in the works on Haṭha-योग. This centre is called अनाहतचक्र since the anāhata sound (sound produced without the beating of two objects) is heard there. It is situated in the region of the heart and is said to have twelve petals of red colour.
For details see CAKRAS.

anavasthā
(‘instability,’ ‘non-finality’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term specially used in Hindu लोगिच्. When the cause and effect series becomes infinite and does not serve as a proof, it is called अनवस्था (infinite regress) and hence rejected.
This अनवस्था is sometimes divided into two varieties: prāmāṇikī or valid, and aprāmāṇikī or invalid. For instance, in the series of बीज (seed) and vṛkṣa (tree) the infinite regress is valid and natural. Hence it is prāmāṇikī. On the other hand, while trying to prove the existence of a cause for this world, if that cause (called ब्रह्मन्) is accepted to have been caused by something else, it leads to अनवस्था, infinite regress, and hence to no definite conclusion. This अनवस्था is aprāmāṇikī or invalid. (To avoid this, Vedānta accepts ब्रह्मन् as the uncaused cause.)

anārabdha
(‘not begun’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism, जैनिस्म् and बुद्धिस्म् are the three world religions which accept the theory of कर्म and reincarnation. According to this theory, the principle, ‘As you sow, so you reap’ can be applied to the field of our actions, both physical and psychical.
‘Karma’ is the unseen effect of an action which will become manifest in course of time under favourable circumstances. This कर्म is of three types: sañcita (‘the accumulated’) or अनारब्ध (‘not begun’), आरब्ध or prārabdha (‘the begun’) and kriyamāṇa (‘being done now’) or āgāmī (‘[giving fruit] in future’).
The entire mass of कर्म which has accumulated over several births, which is yet to fructify, is ‘anārabdha.’ It is from this stock of कर्म, that a part gets ripened and causes the present birth.
Hindu philosophical and religious works declare that आत्मज्ञान (self-realization) can destroy this mass of anārabdhakarma, thus preventing future transmigrations.
The word is also used in its literal sense of anything that is not begun or undertaken.
See also KARMA, PRĀRABDHA, PUNARJANMA, REINCARNATION, SAÑCITA.

Ānarta
------------------------------------------
Ānarta was king of the famous इक्ष्वाकु race, being the grandson of मनु and son of Śaryāti. Sukanyā, the paragon of wifely virtues and wife of the sage च्यवन was his sister. He is said to have built the fortress at the city Kuśasthalī which was later chosen by कृष्ण as his capital under the new name द्वारका.
Vedārtha, a reputed scholar, was his subject.
The country ruled by आनर्त was also called by the same name.

Ānanda Rāmāyaṇa
------------------------------------------
The Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata are the two popular scriptures that have ruled the hearts of the Hindus for millennia. They have inspired innumerable writers, poets and artists to create marvellous works of literature and art based upon the themes drawn from their stories and personalities. One of the numerous Rāmāyaṇas that have sprung up in imita-tion of वाल्मीकि’s is the Ānanda Rāmāyaṇa, sometimes styled as Manohara-आनन्द-Rāmāyaṇa also. Though attributed by tradition to वाल्मीकि himself, it is obviously a late work, later than the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (14th cent. A.D.)
The work comprises 12,323 verses spread over 109 sargas or chapters contained in nine kāṇḍas or books. It is written in the form of a dialogue between पार्वती and शिव, later on introducing another dialogue between two sages रामदास and his disciple Viṣṇudāsa. A few innovations and many additions have been made to the original story as given in वाल्मीकि’s Rāmāyaṇa.
Perhaps, the book was written at a time when the कृष्ण cults were becoming more popular, to reassert the glory and supremacy of राम. Though attempts have been made to establish the identity of the two incarnations and to foresee the events of Kṛṣṇāvatāra in राम’s story, the predisposition in favour of राम is obvious.
An attempt can now be made to summarise the work briefly:
The first book known as Sārakāṇḍa (13 sargas, 2565 ślokas or verses) summarises the entire story of वाल्मीकि’s Rāmāyaṇa, including रावण’s story as given in the last book, Uttarakāṇda. The story of रावण’s bringing the ātmaliṅga of शिव from कैलास and the लिङ्ग being fixed to the ground at गोकर्ण due to the machinations of विष्णु in the guise of a ब्राह्मण boy appears in the 9th sarga. So also the story of establishment of the लिङ्ग at Rāmeśvara. Other additions to the original are: the humbling of Māruti’s pride, the slaying of Airāvaṇa and Mairāvaṇa (friends of रावण from the nether world), the story of कन्याकुमारी and the teaching of Catuśśloki Bhāgavata to व्यास by नारद.
The second book called Yātrākāṇḍa (9 sargas, 746 ślokas) deals with the worship of the river गङ्गा by सीता, the story of the river सरयू and राम’s पिल्ग्रिमगे.
The third book designated Yāga-kāṇḍa (9 sargas, 628 ślokas) describes the Aśvamedhayāga performed by राम along with सीता.
The fourth book, the Vilāsakāṇḍa (9 sargas, 676 ślokas) describes the amorous sports of राम and सीता.
The fifth book named Śubhajanma-kāṇḍa or Janmakāṇḍa (9 sargas, 804 ślokas) deals with the story of the banish-ment of सीता and the birth of लव and कुश to सीता. The interesting points to be noted are: राम deliberately plans and enacts the drama of banishment; कुश is the son born in the natural way to सीता, whereas another baby created by वाल्मीकि out of ‘lava’ seeds (cloves or nutmeg) (hence named ‘Lava’) and infused with life is accepted by सीता as her own son and a special vrata (religious rite) called ‘Saṁyogakaraṇavrata’ is performed by सीता at the behest of वाल्मीकि. The famous Rāmarakṣā Stotra forms part of the 5th sarga.
The sixth book christened Vivāha-kāṇḍa (9 sargas, 585 ślokas) describes the मर्रिअगे of कुश with Campikā and लव with Sumati, as also the मर्रिअगे of Yūpaketu (son of शत्रुघ्न) with Madanasundarī (daughter of the king Kambukaṇṭha). The last section deals with the mūlamantra of आञ्जनेय and the process of repeating it in order to get rid of the maladies due to diseases and evil spirits.
Rājyakāṇḍa (24 sargas, 2641 ślokas), the seventh book, contains some miscellaneous topics like Rāmasahasranāma, the story of a dog and a saṁnyāsin who was given the ‘punishment’ of being made the head of a temple organization, the banning of laughter in his kingdom by राम, the story of वाल्मीकि’s previous births and राम teaching a lesson to सीता and राम’s discourses on धर्म to his subjects. The 8th sarga of this book is completely in prose.
Manoharakāṇḍa (18 sargas, 3101 ślokas) the penultimate book is the largest in volume and contains राम’s expounding spiritual truths to his मोथेर् कौसल्या as also सुमित्रा and कैकेयी, at their request. A number of hymns, technically called ‘kavaca’ (= armour) have been included in this section (Śrīrāmakavaca, Hanūmatkavaca, Sītākavaca and so on). A ritual recitation of these is said to fulfil any desire one cherishes. The 17th sarga gives the story of Rāmāyaṇa in a nutshell and is called Sārarāmāyaṇa.
The last book, with the appellation of Pūrṇakāṇḍa (9 sargas, 577 ślokas) is the smallest in size. It describes राम’s ascent to वैकुण्ठ (the abode of विष्णु) as विष्णु after installing कुश on his throne as his successor.
See also RĀMĀYAṆA and VĀLMĪKI.

anadhyāya
(‘not studying [the वेदस्]’)
------------------------------------------
All those who labour need rest. The system of holidays and vacations is as old as mankind. The Vedic students and their teachers were no exception. अध्ययन or Vedic studies were to be pursued according to some rules and regulations set by tradition. On certain specified days, the आचार्य would not teach. Such days were known as अनध्याय or days of anadhyayana. However, on such days the students were expected to revise their lessons, to do cintana and मनन (reflection) and even get guidance from the senior students.
Days of अनध्याय are: pratipad, aṣṭamī, caturdaśī, pūrṇimā and अमावास्या as also days of saṅkramaṇa. These are—according to the lunar calendar—the 1st, 8th and 14th days after new-मोओन् and full-मोओन्; full-मोओन् and new-मोओन् days, and the days on which the sun enters the next sign of the zodiac.

anātman
(‘the not-self ’ or ‘the non-self ’)
------------------------------------------
‘Who am I?’, ‘Whence did this world originate?’—these are two of the important questions posed by philosophical inquirers. The Vedānta system of philosophy posits the view that the world has evolved out of the आत्मन् (the Self) and it is the same आत्मन् that is our real nature. Everything else is included under the term ‘anātman’. Though literally the external world with its myriads of objects is also अनात्मन्, the word is used more particularly to denote the body, the sense-organs and the मिन्द् which force us to identify ourselves with them, thereby forgetting our आत्मन्-nature.
See also ĀTMAN.

anna-homa
(‘oblation of ड़ोओद्’)
------------------------------------------
Among the several वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् अश्वमेध and वाजपेय are among the better known ones. अन्न-होम is a subsi-diary rite of these sacrifices. It consists mainly of an oblation of ghee, grains and powder of barley and grains of pounded rice, offered into the sacrificial fire just before sunrise. The oblatory materials however, may sometimes differ.

annamaya-kośa
(‘the ड़ोओद्-sheath’)
------------------------------------------
It is the physical body born out of अन्न or ड़ोओद् and nourished by ड़ोओद्. Like a कोश or sheath, it covers the self and prevents the experience of its true nature. It is the first of the five such kośas (pañcakośas). It is destroyed at death. It is also called sthūla-śarīra or the gross body, the first of a series of three śarīras.
See PAÑCAKOŚAS.

annakūṭa
(‘heap of ड़ोओद्’)
------------------------------------------
In the Dīpāvali festival which falls during the months of Āśvina and Kārttika (usually in November), on the third day known as Balipratipad, it is customary to worship the गोवर्धन hill which is near मथुरा (Uttar Pradesh). This is the legendary hill which Śrī कृष्ण as a boy is said to have lifted up on his left little finger to protect the people and cattle of Vṛndāvana from the wrath of इन्द्र who had sent incessant and heavy rains. Those who are not living near this hill are advised to make an image of the hill with cowdung or ड़ोओद्. In the latter case, the heap of ड़ोओद् (anna = ड़ोओद्) is called अन्नकूट and worship is offered to it.
